title: Mixed Game Poker in Canada: Stud, Razz and Draw
excerpt: Mixed game poker rewards players willing to learn beyond Hold'em. Here is how stud, razz and draw variants work, and why Canadian games stay soft.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Almost every Canadian who plays online poker learned Hold'em first, and most never leave. That is precisely why mixed game poker is worth a look: the games are populated by a smaller pool of players, many of whom are only competent in one or two of the formats being dealt, and the skill gap in the less familiar rounds is often enormous. If you are willing to put in a modest amount of study, the rotation formats offer better value per hour than the same stakes in No-Limit Hold'em. This guide explains what is actually in the rotation and how to approach each piece.

What mixed games are and how rotations work

A mixed game rotates through several poker variants at a fixed table, changing either every set number of hands or every orbit. The best-known rotation is HORSE, which cycles through Hold'em, Omaha Hi-Lo, Razz, Seven-Card Stud and Stud Hi-Lo — the E stands for Eight or better, the qualifier used in the split-pot round. Larger rotations add draw variants and pot-limit games.

Nearly all mixed games are played with fixed betting limits rather than no-limit, which changes the texture of the game completely. Pots grow in predictable increments, single hands rarely threaten your whole stack, and the edge comes from making slightly better decisions repeatedly rather than from one large bluff. If your only reference point is no-limit, expect a period of adjustment; our online poker guide covers the fundamentals that carry across all formats.

Seven-Card Stud

Stud is the oldest variant in most rotations and the one where information management matters most. Each player receives two down cards and one up card, then three more up cards and a final down card, betting between each. There is no community board, so every hand is assembled independently.

The defining skill is card reading in the literal sense: tracking which cards have appeared in other players' up cards and folded hands. If you hold three hearts and five hearts are already visible around the table, your flush draw is close to worthless. If you hold a pair of nines and both remaining nines are showing elsewhere, your improvement chances have vanished. Players who do this tracking consistently beat players who do not, and the gap is wider than in any community-card game.

Starting hand priorities in Stud

  • Three of a kind: extremely strong and rare, and should be played for value rather than slow-played into oblivion.
  • Big pairs, ideally hidden: a pair in the hole with a blank up card disguises your strength.
  • Three cards to a flush or straight: playable when live, meaning your needed cards are not already visible elsewhere.
  • Big cards: three high cards have value because they can make the best pair and are hard for opponents to dominate.

Razz

Razz is Seven-Card Stud played for the lowest hand, with straights and flushes ignored and aces counting as low. The best possible hand is five-four-three-two-ace, known as the wheel. It sounds simple, and it is the round where recreational players lose the most money, because the instinct to value high cards is hard to unlearn.

The core Razz discipline is starting hand selection. You want three cards to a strong low, and you want the cards you need to still be available. A hand of two-three-seven is playable; a hand of two-three-nine when three other players show low cards is a trap. Because the game plays out over five betting rounds, entering with a weak low and drawing badly costs multiple bets, and those bets compound over a session far faster than players expect.

The other key adjustment is that Razz hands are often decided by who bricks first. Watching opponents catch high cards on later streets is your cue to apply pressure, even when your own hand is not yet made.

Omaha Hi-Lo

Omaha Hi-Lo splits the pot between the best high hand and the best qualifying low hand, where a low must be eight or better. Each player has four hole cards and must use exactly two of them, which is the rule newcomers most often get wrong.

The winning concept in Hi-Lo is scooping. Hands that can win both halves of the pot are worth far more than hands that can only win one, which is why an ace-two combination with suited connectivity is so much stronger than four high cards. Playing for half a pot while an opponent plays for the whole thing is a slow, grinding way to lose money.

Draw variants

Larger rotations add draw games, most commonly Deuce-to-Seven Triple Draw lowball and Badugi. Both are low-hand games with multiple drawing rounds, and both punish players who cannot count outs accurately.

Triple Draw gives you three opportunities to exchange cards, aiming for the lowest hand with no pairs, straights or flushes. Badugi uses four cards and requires all four to be different suits and different ranks. These are the least-studied games in most rotations, which makes them the softest, but they also require genuine preparation — showing up and improvising is an expensive way to learn.

Why Canadian mixed games stay profitable

Two factors keep the mixed game player pool relatively soft. First, the study burden is real, so most recreational players never bother, and many who do only learn the rounds they enjoy. Second, the fixed-limit structure makes losses feel gradual rather than dramatic, which keeps weaker players in their seats longer than no-limit does.

The practical implication is that you do not need to be excellent at all five games. You need to be solid in the ones most opponents neglect — usually Razz and the stud variants — and merely competent in Hold'em, where everyone is decent. A player who is average in three rounds and clearly better in two will win at a rate that would require far more work to achieve in a pure Hold'em game.

Availability in Canada varies by platform and province. Regulated Ontario operators carry a narrower mixed game selection than the international market, and traffic is thinner at higher stakes, so scheduling matters — evenings and weekends are when the games actually run. Our 888poker Ontario review covers the provincial poker product, and players who enjoy limit-structured decision making may also find our video poker guide a useful companion for understanding fixed-payout thinking.

How to start without lighting money on fire

Pick one non-Hold'em variant and learn it properly before joining a full rotation. Razz is the natural first choice because its rules are the simplest and its strategic principles are the most rapidly learned. Play the lowest available stakes while you build the habit of tracking exposed cards, and accept that your first few sessions are tuition.

Keep your bankroll requirements in mind: fixed-limit games have lower variance per hand than no-limit but you will play more hands to resolution, so a bankroll of several hundred big bets for your chosen stake is a sensible baseline. Review hands afterwards rather than mid-session, and check our latest poker coverage for strategy updates as the Canadian market evolves.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
